title: Radix Sort
tagline: Sort big integers by stacking stable counting sorts, one digit at a time.

intuition.analogy: Old library card sorters physically passed cards through bins by the last digit, restacked, then by the next digit, and so on. After processing every digit position, the cards came out perfectly ordered.
paragraphs: Counting sort is great for small ranges but dies when numbers are large. Radix sort fixes this: instead of sorting by the whole number, it sorts by one digit at a time, from least significant to most significant, using a stable sort (counting sort) at each pass.

Stability is the secret. After sorting by the units digit, numbers with the same tens digit retain their units order. So when you then sort by tens, ties are already correctly ordered by units — and the effect compounds across all digit positions.
With base b digits and d digit positions, you run d stable passes of O(n + b) each. For 32-bit integers using base 256, that's just 4 passes — effectively linear for fixed-width integers.
intuition.keyIdea: Repeatedly stable-sort by each digit, least significant first; stability makes earlier digits act as tie-breakers.

steps.title: Pick a base
steps.detail: Choose base b (e.g. 10 for decimal digits, 256 for bytes). Larger b means fewer passes but bigger count arrays.

steps.title: Stable counting sort per digit
steps.detail: For digit position p (starting at the least significant), extract digit = (x / b^p) % b and stable-counting-sort by it.

steps.title: Repeat for all d positions
steps.detail: After the most significant digit pass, the array is fully sorted.

codes.source:
def radix_sort(a, base=10):
    if not a: return a
    mx = max(a)
    exp = 1
    while mx // exp > 0:
        buckets = [[] for _ in range(base)]
        for x in a:
            buckets[(x // exp) % base].append(x)   # stable
        a = [x for b in buckets for x in b]
        exp *= base
    return a

complexity.timeReason: d passes, each a counting sort costing O(n + b).

pitfalls: Each digit pass MUST be stable, or the algorithm is wrong.
Negative numbers need special handling (sort by sign, or offset).
Choosing too large a base wastes memory; too small increases passes.

dryRun.clickMoment: After the units pass, look at the 4x pair 45 and 75 — once the tens pass runs, their already-correct units order is preserved. Earlier passes silently become tie-breakers.

problems.title: Maximum Gap
problems.statement: Find the largest gap between consecutive sorted elements in linear time.
problems.hint: Radix or bucket sort gives the needed linear-time ordering.

approach: Sort in linear time with LSD radix sort (or bucketing), then a single scan finds the largest gap between consecutive elements.
Radix sort processes digits from least to most significant using stable counting passes, so the total cost is O(d·n) with d the number of digits — effectively O(n).

problems.statement: Answer kth-smallest queries over numbers trimmed to their rightmost digits.
problems.hint: Repeated stable sorting by trailing digits mirrors radix sort.

approach: For each query (index, trim), we rank numbers by their last `trim` characters. A stable LSD radix sort over those trailing digits reproduces the required ordering while keeping original indices on ties.
Process the trimmed suffix digit by digit from the rightmost; stability preserves earlier order so equal trimmed values stay in original index order.

problems.title: Sort Integers by Number of 1 Bits
problems.statement: Sort by popcount, ties by value.
problems.hint: A stable sort by primary then secondary key echoes radix layering.

approach: Sort by a composite key (popcount, value). This is a stable multi-key sort — exactly what radix/bucket sorting expresses naturally.
Simplest correct form: key each number by bit-count*100000 + value (values <= 10^4), then sort. Equal popcounts fall back to numeric order.

problems.title: Largest Number
problems.statement: Arrange numbers to form the largest concatenation.
problems.hint: Custom comparator; understand why a stable, well-defined ordering matters.

approach: Arrange numbers so their concatenation is largest. Sort with a custom comparator: a before b iff a+b > b+a (string concatenation).
After sorting descending by that rule, join. Guard the all-zeros case so the result is "0" not "00…0".

codes.source:
from functools import cmp_to_key
class Solution:
    def largestNumber(self, nums: list[int]) -> str:
        s = list(map(str, nums))
        s.sort(key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: (a + b < b + a) - (a + b > b + a)))
        res = ''.join(s)
        return '0' if res[0] == '0' else res
